paras: The attempted lynching of William Riley and Andrew Kelly took place at Asbury Park, New Jersey, on the night of July 5, 1903, when citizens of nearby Eatontown set out to seize the two Black men from the Neptune township lockup after they were charged with running down a young white woman on a bicycle. The township police chief guarded the jail and moved the prisoners to the county jail at Freehold, and the crowd dispersed. Coming the same week as the Evansville riot, the case was cited in several editorials as proof that mob law had spread to the North.

On Saturday, July 4, Miss Jennie Covert of Eatontown was struck on the Eatontown road while riding her bicycle by a carriage or wagon carrying Black men and a woman. According to the wire report, the occupants, "it is claimed," cursed her and drove on, leaving her on the roadway. She was carried unconscious to the hospital at Long Branch, where she was reported near death, and a second automobile of men chased the carriage without success.

Riley and Kelly, described as colored men of West Park, were arrested in West Asbury Park on Sunday and lodged in the township jail. When Covert's friends in Eatontown learned of the capture, they went looking for wagons and vehicles to carry men to Asbury Park to storm the jail. In the wire version, "stages and carriages were soon loaded with determined men" and made the run to the jail on South Main Street.

Warned of the crowd's intention, Chief Walter H. Gravatt of the Neptune township police surrounded the jail with his men and had the prisoners arraigned before Magistrate Dodd, who held them without bail to await the outcome of Covert's injuries. Handcuffed together, they were driven in a closed carriage to the county jail at Freehold, by the Sun's account at midnight. Some in the crowd wanted to pursue the police, but the officers had a good start, and the throng gradually dispersed.

No arrest of anyone in the crowd appears in the coverage. On November 2, 1903, Andrew Kelly, Wm. Reilly and Lizzie Reilly, "all colored," were tried in Monmouth County Court before Judge Heisley on an indictment for assault and battery on Carrie Covert in Eatontown. Reilly, as the driver in control of the wagon, was found guilty, and the court directed the acquittal of Kelly and Lizzie Reilly. At sentencing, lawyer A. J. C. Stokes presented a petition from Asbury Park business men asking for leniency, and Reilly received one year in State Prison.

New York papers carried the story on July 6 and 7, with the Evening World headlining "Asbury Park Lynching Mob Misses Prisoners" and the Sun "Ready to Lynch Two Negroes." These reports credited the police chief and largely treated the charge as fact, the Sun stating that the men left Covert "bleeding and senseless." The Alexandria Gazette ran the wire story as "Lynching Frustrated" and, in an editorial the same day, listed Asbury Park beside Evansville and Linton as signs of "the rapid growth of mob law."

The Sun's editorial "The Lynching Craze" used the case to argue that the mob spirit existed "in quiet New Jersey towns," describing the Asbury Park crowd as "a mob of respectable farmers." The Evening Star in Washington and the Wichita Daily Eagle reprinted that passage, and a condensed brief reached small papers in Wisconsin and South Dakota by late July. In Maryland, the Westminster Democratic Advocate cited the case under the heading "The North Takes Up Lynching," in an editorial that also defended curtailing Black suffrage in the South.
The only Black-press notice found was a single sentence in the Baltimore Afro-American's news column on July 11, naming no one and giving no outcome.

The wire story counted three arrested men and listed Walter H. Gravatt among them, although it also named him as the police chief who protected the prisoners; the Tribune and the Sun named only Riley and Kelly. The county court record names the third defendant as a woman, Lizzie Reilly, and gives the injured woman's first name as Carrie. Accounts also differ on whether the crowd reached the jail: the wire story says it did and "clamored about the court," while the Tribune describes only a plan that the chief's action foiled.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of William Riley and Andrew Kelly
bases: Wire reports describe Eatontown citizens setting out to take three Black prisoners from the Asbury Park lockup to lynch them, foiled when police moved the men to the county jail (A1, A3, A5).

No one was killed: the prisoners were moved to Freehold and later tried in county court (A3, A13); the episode was an attempted lynching by a crowd of Eatontown citizens acting to punish the men for running down Jennie Covert (A1, A5).

The Evening World wire story (A1, A5), the Tribune's own telegraph (A2) and the Sun's report (A3) agree on the arrest, the Eatontown movement against the jail and the removal to Freehold, and the Monmouth Inquirer's court reports (A13, A14) confirm the charge and trial.

accounts.label: Wire report (Evening World / Alexandria Gazette)
accounts.gist: Eatontown citizens loaded stages and carriages and ran to the jail; the chief surrounded it, had the men arraigned and drove them to Freehold 'while the crowd clamored about the court', after which the throng dispersed.

accounts.label: Tribune telegraph
accounts.gist: There was 'a movement on foot' among Covert's friends to visit the lockup in a body; the chief's prompt action foiled the plan and 'cooler judgment prevailed' once the men were in the county jail.

accounts.label: Sun report
accounts.gist: Eatontown residents went looking for wagons to storm the jail; the prisoners were driven to Freehold at midnight and the Eatontown people 'turned back with regret'.

accounts.label: Black press brief
accounts.gist: A mob wanted to lynch three negroes who had run down a young lady on a bicycle 'with serious results'.

accounts.label: County court record
accounts.gist: The three Black defendants were tried for assault and battery on Carrie Covert; only the driver was convicted.

framing.detail: The Evening World headlined 'Asbury Park Lynching Mob Misses Prisoners' and credited the police chief, while repeating the charge that the men 'deliberately' ran the girl down.
The Sun's news story ('Ready to Lynch Two Negroes') stated as fact that the men ran over Covert and left her 'bleeding and senseless', and noted the Eatontown people were 'much disappointed'.
The Sun's editorial 'The Lynching Craze' used Asbury Park's 'mob of respectable farmers' to argue that the mob spirit existed 'in quiet New Jersey towns' and 'must stop'.
The Evening Star and Wichita Daily Eagle reprinted the Sun's editorial passage weeks later.
The Alexandria Gazette listed Asbury Park among signs of 'the rapid growth of mob law in the United States'.
The Westminster Democratic Advocate's 'The North Takes Up Lynching' cited the case to argue the North had 'gotten into the lynching business' while defending curtailed Black suffrage in the South.
The Baltimore Afro-American gave it one unadorned sentence in a general news column, next to an item on the 'reign of terror' in Evansville.

Citizens of Eatontown, friends of Miss Covert ('a mob of respectable farmers' in the Sun's editorial); no individuals named.
Pursuit (automobile chase before the arrest) and a threatened descent on the jail; whether the crowd reached and besieged the jail is contested.
Supported for the arrest and the night gathering; the accident was Saturday, July 4.
Riley (Reilly) was convicted of assault and battery on Nov. 2, 1903, and sentenced to one year in State Prison; Kelly and Lizzie Reilly were acquitted.

info: Covert was run down on Saturday, July 4, 1903; the men were arrested on Sunday, July 5, and the Eatontown crowd gathered that night, with the prisoners removed to Freehold at midnight or the next morning.

Accident on the Eatontown road at Eatontown; arrest in West Asbury Park; threatened jail was the Neptune township lockup on South Main Street, Asbury Park; prisoners moved to the county jail at Freehold.

William Riley (Reilly) and Andrew Kelly (Kelley), both 'colored', of West Park; the wire story counts three and adds 'Walter H. Gravatt', the name of the police chief; a woman was with them and was later tried as Lizzie Reilly.

Charged with running over Miss Jennie Covert of Eatontown, who was riding a bicycle, and leaving her unconscious on the road; 'it is claimed' they cursed her; she lay unconscious in the Long Branch hospital and was not expected to live.
